statement: A pizza shop offers 7 different vegetable toppings and 4 different meat toppings. Lea orders a pizza with exactly three different toppings: two vegetables and one meat. How many different pizzas could she order?

choices.misconception: I counted the two vegetables as $7 \times 6$, so each pair was counted twice, once in each order.
I chose any 3 of the 11 toppings and ignored the rule of two vegetables and one meat.
I added the 21 pairs of vegetables and the 4 meats instead of multiplying.
I counted every three-topping pizza with at least two vegetables, which also adds the 35 pizzas with three vegetables.

hints: Choose the vegetables and the meat separately.
Picking two vegetables is a selection, so their order does not matter. Then each pair of vegetables can go with any meat.

solutions.reliable: The pair of vegetables can be chosen in $\frac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21$ ways, dividing by 2 because the order of the two does not matter. The meat can be chosen in 4 ways. Each pair works with each meat, so there are $21 \times 4 = 84$ pizzas. The transferable idea: count each independent selection on its own, then multiply.

whyOnTest: Selections where order does not matter, combined across two groups, test both dividing out order and multiplying independent choices.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
